abstracts.W7223235916: Non-exhaust vehicle emissions (brake wear, tire wear, and road dust) now dominate particulate matter (PM) sources in urban environments as tailpipe emissions continue to decline. Among these, brake wear particles (BWPs) remain under-characterized, particularly their organic composition. This study investigates the formation and atmospheric relevance of amines released during the thermal degradation of phenolic resin, the primary binder in brake pads. Controlled brake dynamometer and phenolic-resin thermal degradation experiments were performed together with field measurements adjacent to two Southern California freeways (I-5, Santa Ana, and I-710, Long Beach). High-resolution mass spectrometry analysis revealed the prevalence of nitrogen-containing compounds across all datasets, with dicyclohexylamine (DCHA) consistently detected in laboratory and ambient particles. DCHA concentrations in laboratory particles ranged from 0.08–1.6 ng/ug across brake pad types and resin conditions. DCHA was measured in air sampled onto filters at levels ranging from 2.1+/-1.6 pg m-3 (Santa Ana) to 3.5+/-1.7 pg m-3 (Long Beach). Ambient levels of DCHA correlated strongly with near-road NO and brake-associated metals (Fe, Ba), suggesting a possible link between its emission and braking activity. These findings identify brake wear as a previously under-recognized source of DCHA and related organic nitrogen compounds, often attributed primarily to tire wear emissions.
abstracts.W7223695639: The ingestion of microplastics by fish is widely documented, but the drivers of contamination and the movement of particles within organisms are still not well understood. We investigated microplastic contamination in sport fish caught from San Francisco Bay in California, USA. We compared microplastic contamination in striped bass (Morone saxatilis) and shiner surfperch (Cymatogaster aggregata). We observed an average of 5.9 ± 5.6 (Std Dev) microplastics per fish, with significantly higher overall contamination in striped bass but higher concentrations (microplastics/gram of tissue) in shiner surfperch. For each, we considered contamination relevant to their consumption by recreational anglers. For striped bass, where only the fillet is typically ingested, we found that contamination among tissues differed significantly (on average 3.8 ± 3.1 microplastics/fish fillets). Shiner surfperch, which are typically consumed whole, had an average body burden of 9.1 ± 1.2 microplastics/fish. Contamination varied significantly (p-value < 0.0001) among sampling locations for shiner surfperch, with the highest amounts observed near urban centers (no significant spatial pattern was observed for striped bass). Our findings show microplastics in tissues beyond the gastrointestinal tract, posing concerns for fish health and suggesting that fish caught from San Francisco Bay are a pathway for human consumption of microplastics.
abstracts.W7223808838: Atmospheric deposition of microplastics (MPs) at an event-scale resolution can be measured in snowfall events, as snow scavenges atmospheric MPs and the snowpack serves as a repository for MP accumulation. We monitored MP deposition in freshly fallen snow, the snowpack, and dry deposition over the course of 6 months in the Sierra Nevada of North America. Average microplastic concentrations in fresh snow ranged from 11.8 to 37.5 p/L at remote sites, which were significantly less than the 68.3 to 92.9 p/L MP concentrations found at the anthropogenically impacted site. Average bulk deposition rates were estimated to be 267 to 3190 p/m2/day at remote sites, significantly lower than the 3242 to 7480 p/m2/day at the anthropogenically impacted site. HYSPLIT back-trajectory modeling characterized the potential regional transport of MPs from upwind regions that were predominantly agricultural and suburban areas, as well as localized anthropogenic activities that could significantly affect MP deposition rates in snowfall. This study introduces high-throughput FTIR analysis methods with a highlight on fiber spectroscopy, demonstrates the value of estimating MP fluxes at the meteorological event scale, reports MP deposition rates in a critical water resource, and provides a basis for future long-term atmospheric MP monitoring.
abstracts.W7223933094: Tire-wear particles release diverse additive mixtures into aquatic environments, but the formulation-level drivers of species-specific molecular toxicity remain poorly resolved. Here, we combined full factorial design, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate the predicted molecular toxicity potential of 96 styrene-butadiene rubber tire-additive schemes across three coexisting Daphnia species ( D. pulex , D. magna , and D. galeata ), using arginine kinase as an energy-metabolism target protein. Binding-energy-based responses varied substantially among additive schemes and species. The largest differences between the highest- and lowest-predicted toxicity schemes reached 69.3% for D. pulex , 75.8% for D. magna , and 76.3% for D. galeata . Across the tested schemes, D. magna showed the strongest predicted sensitivity, whereas D. galeata generally showed the weakest. Scheme A3B2C2D1E2F2 produced the greatest interspecific divergence, with stronger predicted molecular interaction potential in D. magna than in D. pulex or D. galeata . Full factorial analysis indicated that additive effects were not strictly additive, with higher-order interactions contributing to species-specific response patterns. Antioxidant-related factors, particularly aniline antioxidant-associated components, were more frequently linked to elevated predicted toxicity potential. Molecular interaction analysis showed that van der Waals forces dominated additive–arginine kinase binding, while changes in polar and nonpolar residue contributions suggested a secondary role for hydrophilic interactions. Overall, this study provides a formulation-level computational screening framework for prioritizing tire-additive combinations with lower predicted molecular toxicity potential and for guiding future experimental validation of safer tire formulations.
abstracts.W7224814620: Abstract Rivers act as both major pathways for marine plastic pollution and as important features for the storage and burial of plastic pollution. To better understand plastic emissions from watersheds to the ocean, we measured retention and remobilization of floating plastic bottles in rivers using Global Positioning System (GPS) tracking across 30 river reaches in 7 coastal watersheds throughout the United States and southern Canada. Movement data revealed that mobilization events and travel distances were related to river discharge, reach geomorphology, and upstream land cover. Bottles moved an average of 6.1 km (min. 73 m, max. 53.5 km) over a mean deployment period of 87 days. Bottle mobilization events were related to specific stream power and the time a bottle remained lodged prior to a high-flow event. Mobilization distance increased with discharge, decreased with forest cover, and increased with urban cover (all with p < 0.001). A probabilistic model estimated that 50% of bottles that reach the ocean or the Great Lakes in any given year originated from more than 15.7( ± 0.8) km inland and up to 200 km. Our results suggest that cleanups and efforts to prevent plastic pollution from entering urban rivers in coastal watersheds are vital to help curb ever-increasing marine plastic pollution.
abstracts.W7224937136: Microplastics undergo continued physicochemical transformation under environmental stresses such as mechanical abrasion, thermal cycling, and ultraviolet (UV) radiation. However, their degradation is commonly evaluated using population-averaged or independent endpoint measurements, which cannot directly reveal how individual particles evolve over time or how degradation trajectories differ among particles. Here, we longitudinally tracked the degradation of individual poly(ethylene terephthalate) microplastics (PET MPs) during 45 days of accelerated UV-C aging. Low-vacuum scanning electron microscopy (LV-SEM) and high-magnification digital microscopy (DM) enabled repeated morphological characterization of the same particles, while atomic force microscopy (AFM) PinPoint™ mapping provided particle-level measurements of nanoscale surface roughness and local apparent Young’s modulus. The nine tracked PET MPs exhibited markedly heterogeneous degradation trajectories: after 45 days, seven particles retained approximately 25–56% of their initial projected area, whereas two had no detectable projected area remaining. Mean fractional area loss increased across successive 15-day intervals, indicating increasing susceptibility to material loss with accumulated aging. Associations between particle morphology and subsequent material loss also varied across aging intervals, although these relationships are considered exploratory given the small particle population. AFM measurements further revealed substantial local nanomechanical heterogeneity and an overall decrease in apparent Young’s modulus from Day 0 to Day 45. These results highlight the value of longitudinal same-particle measurements for resolving both temporal evolution and particle-to-particle heterogeneity during accelerated PET microplastic degradation.
abstracts.W7225619797: Anthropogenic microparticles, including microplastics, have become a pervasive, global environmental issue in all biomes. In marine systems, their impacts on large pelagic predators remain poorly quantified, limiting our ability to understand exposure pathways and ecological consequences. Salmon sharks ( Lamna ditropis ), regionally endothermic predators in the North Pacific, may be vulnerable to microparticle ingestion due to their high energetic demands, broad diet, and exploitation of coastal and offshore habitats known to contain relatively high amounts of pollution. To assess exposure in this species, we analyzed stomachs from 18 salmon sharks collected off the Oregon coast between 2022 and 2024 and evaluated differences across ontogenetic and sex classes as well as microparticle counts in their prey. Anthropogenic microparticles were found in every shark stomach, with an average (± SD) of 25.6 ± 23.0 microparticles per stomach. Anthropogenic microparticles were dominated by fibers and fragments, with white and black being the most common colors. µFTIR spectroscopy confirmed approximately 16% of anthropogenic microparticles were synthetic polymers, primarily polyethylene, polypropylene, and polyamide, while the remainder consisted largely of anthropogenic cellulose with spectra most similar to cotton. Microplastics were detected in all but three stomachs, yielding an 82.4% detection frequency of plastics. Relative to other elasmobranch studies, salmon sharks exhibited universally high detection frequencies and elevated particle burdens. This study provides the first evidence of microplastics and anthropogenic microparticle ingestion in salmon sharks and contributes to the growing body of literature documenting exposure in large pelagic predators.
abstracts.W7225641200: Abstract Polyethylene plastic mulch (PE mulch) has been increasingly used by specialty crop growers to improve crop yield and quality. However, most PE mulch after use ends up in landfills, causing plastic pollution. The challenge of recycling agricultural PE mulch waste is due to its high contaminant content. To address this challenge and promote the recycling of PE mulch, this study explored the processing of PE mulch waste and used it as a modifier in asphalt paving materials. The results of performance tests showed that the addition of PE mulch stiffened asphalt binders, which benefited rutting resistance, but slightly compromised cracking resistance. Recycled PE mulch had a lower effectiveness to modify asphalt binders than virgin PE mulch because of its lower effective plastic content. The dry mixing method is recommended to incorporate PE mulch waste into mixtures, as it has a lower adverse effect on cracking resistance than the wet mixing method.
abstracts.W850579650: Packaging Materials account for 31% of the world’s municipal solid waste. Agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR) are pushing for the increased use of recycled thermoplastic materials. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is a commonly recycled thermoplastic which is used to package ready-to-eat fruits and vegetables. Most recycled polyethylene terephthalate (RPET) packaging materials contain heavy metal catalysts, the most common being antimony. The recent increased use of recycled plastic materials has been suspected as the source of increased human heavy metal exposure. In this study, cadmium, chromium, nickel, lead and antimony were quantified in post-consumer RPET rigid containers and films using inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometry (ICP-AES). Two hundred samples were tested of which 29 were found to be contaminated with heavy metals in the parts-per-million (ppm) range. Chromium was found in all the contaminated sample replicates at an average level of 8.18 ppm. Cadmium was found in all the contaminated samples as well. Lead was found in 90.4% of the contaminated samples and concentrations ranged from a low of 0.02 ppm to a high of 0.36 ppm. Nickel was found in 96.4% of the contaminated samples while antimony was found in 97.6% of the samples. Due to limited sample material, 22 of the 29 contaminated RPET rigid containers and films were tested for heavy metal migration into a 5% citric acid:water solution (w/v) or deionized water. Samples were subjected to prolonged storage at 7.2 or 22.2°C for 1, 7 or 14 days, or were exposed for 5 minutes to microwaves from a 1700-watt microwave oven set to 70% power before analysis. Leachate values were at ppb levels but were often below the ICP-AES Limits of Detection which were at also the ppb level, whether calculated for deionized water or 5% citric acid in water. No measureable levels of heavy metal were detected for any sample exposed to water, regardless of treatment. For samples exposed to 5% citrate and stored or microwaved, only chromium and nickel leached at measurable levels, and the number of RPET’s releasing measurable chromium and nickel increased with microwaving compared to the same plastics stored at 22.2 or 7.2°C. Since leaching was calculated as µg/L of heavy metal lost from the entire inner surface (1021 cm2) of a retail salad bag, actual exposure to heavy metal would be much less than measured in this study as retail
